column2: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems) v2026.08
column7: - ATLAS maps adversary tactics and techniques against AI-enabled systems, AI capability abuse, and harmful autonomous behavior backed by case studies and red-team evidence · - Content release v2026.08 adds agentic techniques (AML.T0116 through AML.T0128) and renames AI Attack Staging to AI Attack Adaptation · - Monthly content releases (YYYY.MM) are separate from data format semver (6.0.0); manifest ties versions in GitHub atlas-data · - Platforms field on techniques tags Predictive AI, Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Enterprise scope
column8: - Living taxonomy: same technique ID may gain sub-techniques or maturity labels without changing the core attack story · - Navigator layers and STIX exports reflect the selected content version; diff releases rather than a single static PDF · - Case studies lag real-world agent deployments; technique maturity marks emerging vs validated entries
column9: - Map production AI controls and detections to ATLAS techniques and mitigations during threat modeling · - Subscribe to mitre-atlas/atlas-data releases and patch local Navigator layers when v2026.08 or later ships · - Use case studies as test scenarios for red teams; contribute new cases through ATLAS submission workflows · - Pair ATLAS agentic techniques with OWASP Agentic Top 10 and MCP-specific controls where tools and memory appear

column2: ETSI EN 304 223 V2.1.1 — Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems
column7: - European baseline for deployable AI systems using deep neural networks, including generative AI, across the full lifecycle · - Thirteen principles in five phases: secure design, development, deployment, maintenance, and end of life · - Addresses AI-specific risks: data poisoning, model obfuscation, indirect prompt injection, and training-data handling gaps · - Signposts ISO/IEC 22989 lifecycle stages, ETSI TR 104 128 implementation guide, and TS 104 216 conformance assessment
column8: - Out of scope for research-only AI never intended for deployment · - Does not replace ISO/IEC 27001; maps to existing cyber programs rather than duplicating generic IT controls · - Modal verbs follow ETSI drafting rules (shall/should/may); must/must not do not appear in deliverables
column9: - Assign lifecycle owners for each of the thirteen principles from design through model disposal · - Run asset identification and supply-chain tracking for data, models, prompts, and training infrastructure (Principles 5–8) · - Test and evaluate before release; monitor behavior in production; patch and mitigate on a cadence (Principles 9–12) · - Document end-user and affected-entity communications at deployment; dispose data and models at end of life (Principles 10, 13)

column2: ENISA's view on Cybersecurity in the Frontier AI Era
column7: - Frontier AI compresses discovery-to-exploitation windows; industry data cited puts weaponisation near 15 minutes and median exfiltration near 72 minutes after access · - Negative time-to-exploit: attackers may hold working exploits before vendor fixes ship, especially when patches reveal flaws in unsupported versions · - Defenders must treat environments as potentially compromised and extend ML-based prevention to agentic endpoints and enterprise browsers · - Security fundamentals stay central: asset inventory, patching discipline, segmentation, monitoring, and coordinated disclosure at machine speed
column8: - Position paper, not a binding regulation; recommendations will align to a future European Commission action plan · - Open-source maintainers and SMEs face report-volume spikes from AI-generated findings; triage capacity becomes the bottleneck · - Change-advisory workflows cannot approve fixes quickly enough when exploit windows are minutes; governance must allow faster intervention
column9: - Shift effort from discovery volume to risk-based prioritisation with faster triage and remediation · - Target single-digit-minute MTTD, MTTR, and MTTC where feasible; automate patching and containment paths · - Embed continuous threat modeling with AI-assisted simulation against live architectures · - Integrate defensive AI across SDLC and incident response with humans retained in approval loops · - Prepare CRA Single Reporting Platform workflows assuming active exploitation when awareness begins

column2: Security-Focused Guide for AI Code Assistant Instructions
column7: - Custom instructions (Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, CLAUDE.md, and similar) steer AI code assistants toward secure output · - Developers remain accountable for generated code; AI output requires the same review, test, and SAST discipline as human-written code · - Instructions should stay concise and project-specific; irrelevant security text increases wrong or over-fit code · - Recursive Criticism and Improvement (RCI) loops ask the assistant to review and fix its own prior output with linters and scanners
column8: - Instructions do not replace ASVS, SCVS, or AISVS verification; they reduce common assistant mistakes only · - Persona prompts like act as a security expert often degrade results in cited experiments · - Assistant-suggested dependencies may be hallucinated or outdated; pin versions and verify packages
column9: - Encode input validation, output encoding, secrets handling, and least-privilege defaults in project instruction files · - Require parameterized queries, constant-time comparisons for secrets, and secure error handling without leaking internals · - Mandate SBOM generation, dependency scanning, and CI SAST/DAST in generated pipeline snippets · - Add language-specific rules (bounds-checked C, no shell=True in Python subprocess, pinned container digests with cosign verification)

column2: Emerging Security Practices for AI Agents
column7: - Agent security spans model, system guardrails, harness orchestration, and tool access; each layer needs distinct controls · - Primary attack vectors: prompt injection, memory poisoning, and tool supply-chain compromise where tool output re-enters reasoning · - Misaligned benign requests can cause harm without an external attacker when scope and permissions are too broad · - Shared responsibility across developers, deployers, tool providers, third-party surfaces, and users who grant authority
column8: - Probabilistic model defenses alone cannot guarantee safety; deterministic limits on tools and egress must sit outside the reasoning loop · - Persistent memory propagates poisoned state across turns and agents; harness logging is the enforcement and audit point · - MCP and similar protocols do not guarantee secure implementations; discipline at integration time determines exposure
column9: - Apply least privilege on tools, filesystem, network egress, and credentials; sandbox execution environments · - Block the lethal trifecta: do not combine private-data access, untrusted content, and external communication in one agent without mitigations · - Require human confirmation before irreversible or high-stakes actions; adapt oversight for multi-agent parallel workflows · - Vet tools in directories or sandboxes; combine instruction hierarchies, classifiers, and provenance-aware interpreters such as CaMeL where feasible

column2: Managing Advanced Cyber Risks in Frontier AI Frameworks
column7: - Maps how frontier AI safety frameworks set cyber capability thresholds, assess models, and deploy mitigations · - Dual-use cyber capabilities help defenders patch and detect while lowering barriers for offensive misuse · - Emerging consensus thresholds: non-expert uplift for sophisticated attacks and end-to-end autonomous cyber operations · - Zero-day discovery and attacks against hardened targets are explicit escalation markers across member frameworks
column8: - Threshold wording (significant, meaningful, material uplift) remains subjective; cross-vendor comparability is incomplete · - Benchmarks saturate and suffer contamination; CTF and cyber-range scores may reflect training exposure not operational risk · - Defender benefit from the same model capabilities must weigh into release decisions, not offense alone
column9: - Threat-model AI-cyber paths with ATT&CK, Cyber Kill Chain, and STRIDE; update models as incidents and assessments arrive · - Run tiered capability assessments: knowledge benchmarks, agent CTF/cyber-range tasks, safeguard evals, and expert red teams · - Tie assessment results to output policies, refusals, and monitoring for vulnerability-query and exploit-development patterns · - Document assumptions on actor skill, target hardening, and autonomy before crossing published capability thresholds

column2: Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment
column7: - Tailored checklists for model capability tier (frontier vs general purpose) crossed with release type (restricted API, closed, open) · - Covers R&D risk scanning, pre-deployment safeguards, post-deployment monitoring, and decommission paths · - Expanded 2024 guidance assigns obligations across adapters, hosting services, and application developers in open-model chains · - Significant capability updates after deployment trigger renewed governance, not one-time sign-off
column8: - Voluntary guidance meant to complement regulation such as EU GPAI Code of Practice, not replace legal duties · - Third-party audit methods and incident-reporting baselines remain immature across the industry · - Research or limited releases may warrant lighter oversight than wide public deployment of frontier models
column9: - Select the checklist matching model capability and release type on the Model Deployment Guidance site · - Implement access controls, rate limits, terms of use, and architecture-embedded safety before external release · - Monitor for misuse, jailbreaks, and downstream impacts; define restrict, suspend, and retire criteria · - Publish model cards and downstream safety tooling for open releases; distribute responsibility across the value chain

column2: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI v1.5
column7: - Voluntary Singapore framework for deploying agents built in-house or via third-party platforms · - Four dimensions: assess and bound risks upfront, meaningful human accountability, technical lifecycle controls, end-user responsibility · - Agent components include model, instructions, memory, planning, tools, protocols, access controls, guardrails, approvals, and logging · - v1.5 adds multi-agent and third-party agent risks, automation bias practices, and operational case studies
column8: - Continuous human approval for every agent step does not scale; define checkpoints for high-stakes and irreversible actions only · - Multi-agent architectures diffuse accountability unless roles are mapped across the agentic value chain · - Protocols (MCP, A2A, commerce protocols) evolve quickly; controls must track new tool and agent interaction surfaces
column9: - Bound action-space up front: limit tools, permissions, reversibility, and autonomy per use case · - Assign responsibilities across platform providers, system integrators, and app developers before deployment · - Test agents for execution accuracy, policy adherence, and tool use pre-release; monitor continuously post-release · - Disclose agent scope to users; train operators to resist automation bias and maintain override and audit trails · - Validate alignment with AI Verify toolkit and ISO/IEC 42001 crosswalk where attestations are required
